DOCUMENT:
Internal Audit Memo: Missed Appointments in Outpatient Physiotherapy
To: Director of Operations, Therapies Division
From: Clinical Audit Team
Date: 14 August 2026

1. Scope
This audit examined missed appointments in the outpatient physiotherapy service across our three clinic sites between 1 January and 30 June 2026. For the purposes of this audit, a "did not attend" (DNA) is recorded when a patient fails to attend without giving notice. Late cancellations (less than 24 hours' notice) are recorded and reported separately, because the slot can sometimes be offered to another patient. We reviewed the appointment system records for all 24,860 booked appointments in the period and interviewed reception and clinical staff at each site.

2. Overall position
There were 2,610 DNAs in the period, a DNA rate of 10.5%, against the service target of 8%. Each DNA leaves a 30-minute clinical slot unused. At the service's average cost per clinical hour of £62, the 1,305 lost clinical hours represent around £80,900 of clinical time over six months.

Table 1. DNA rate by appointment type
Appointment type | Booked | DNAs | DNA rate
New patient assessment | 6,210 | 410 | 6.6%
Follow-up | 18,650 | 2,200 | 11.8%
Total | 24,860 | 2,610 | 10.5%

Follow-up appointments account for most DNAs. Staff told us that many patients stop attending once their symptoms improve, without telling the service.

3. Reminder calls
Since 2024, reception staff have phoned patients two working days before their appointment where time allows. In the audit period, staff made reminder calls for 7,800 appointments, about 300 a week over the 26 weeks. A call is recorded as received only if the patient answered and confirmed they would attend; unanswered calls are not recorded. Reception staff estimate that each call, including dialling, rescheduling where needed and updating the record, takes an average of four minutes.

Table 2. DNA rate by reminder status
Reminder status | Appointments | DNAs | DNA rate
Reminder call received | 7,800 | 470 | 6.0%
No reminder call recorded | 17,060 | 2,140 | 12.5%

Patients who received a reminder call were less than half as likely to miss their appointment. Reminder calls therefore more than halve the DNA rate, and extending them to all appointments would bring the service well within its 8% target.

4. Discharge policy
The service's policy is that a patient who DNAs twice without explanation is discharged back to their referrer. We found the policy was applied inconsistently: of 160 patients who met the criterion, 104 were discharged. Staff were reluctant to discharge patients they knew to be vulnerable.

5. Late cancellations
In addition to the DNAs above, 1,140 appointments were cancelled with less than 24 hours' notice. Reception staff were able to refill 31% of these slots, usually with patients on the cancellation list.

6. Findings and recommendations
Finding 1. The DNA rate of 10.5% (including late cancellations, which we classify as DNAs) is above target and costs the service around £80,900 in clinical time every six months.
Recommendation 1. Extend reminder calls to all booked appointments, about 960 a week, using reception staff. This can be absorbed within existing reception hours at no additional cost.

Finding 2. The two-DNA discharge policy is applied inconsistently.
Recommendation 2. Revise the policy to include a documented clinical review before discharge, so that vulnerable patients are protected and the policy can then be applied consistently.

Finding 3. Late-cancellation slots are refilled only 31% of the time.
Recommendation 3. Introduce an automated text offer to patients on the cancellation list when a slot becomes free.

7. Conclusion
Missed appointments are costly but largely preventable. Reminder calls have been shown to more than halve DNAs in this service, and extending them to every patient, together with the policy and process changes above, should bring the DNA rate below target within six months.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "The DNA rate of 10.5% (including late cancellations, which we classify as DNAs)" -- Section 1 defines DNAs as failures to attend without notice and says late cancellations are recorded and reported separately (and section 5 reports 1,140 late cancellations 'in addition to the DNAs above'). Finding 1 says the 10.5% includes late cancellations classified as DNAs. The definition contradicts itself.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "Reminder calls therefore more than halve the DNA rate" -- A call is only recorded as 'received' if the patient answered and confirmed attendance; unanswered calls fall into the comparison group. The groups are selected on engagement/intention to attend, and calls were made only 'where time allows', so the 6.0% vs 12.5% difference does not show the calls caused the reduction.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "This can be absorbed within existing reception hours at no additional cost." -- The document states each call takes about four minutes and staff currently make about 300 calls a week. Going to about 960 a week adds about 660 calls, roughly 44 extra staff hours a week (more than one full-time post). The memo never addresses this workload/cost although its own data raise it.

REVIEW:
# Review: Missed Appointments in Outpatient Physiotherapy

The memo is clearly structured, and the arithmetic is sound: every rate, total and the £80,900 figure check out. But the headline finding, that reminder calls more than halve DNAs, doesn't hold up. The data in Section 3 can't support it, and the main recommendation depends on it. There is also a definitional contradiction in Finding 1 and an unsupported "no additional cost" claim. These should be fixed before the memo goes to the Director.

## Major issues

### 1. The reminder-call comparison is biased by how calls are recorded

Section 3 says: *"A call is recorded as received only if the patient answered and confirmed they would attend; unanswered calls are not recorded."*

This means the 6.0% group is not "patients who were called." It is **patients who were reachable and had just told us they were coming**. The 12.5% group mixes patients who were never called with patients who were called but didn't answer. The groups differ in at least three ways besides the call itself:

- **Self-selection by confirmation.** A patient who has just confirmed is, almost by definition, likely to attend. Someone who has already decided to stop coming is more likely to ignore the phone or not pick up.
- **Unanswered calls fall into the comparison group.** Hard-to-reach patients, who probably have higher DNA risk, inflate the 12.5%.
- **Non-random allocation.** Calls are made "where time allows." Busier sessions, sites or days may differ systematically.

**Possible confounding by appointment type.** New patient assessments have a 6.6% DNA rate, close to the 6.0% seen in the called group. If calls went disproportionately to new patients, much of the apparent effect could just reflect case mix. The memo should break Table 2 down by appointment type (and ideally by site).

Analysing the full record does make the rates *exact as descriptions*. It does not remove these biases. Completeness and causal validity are separate questions. The comparison shows an association; it does not show that calls cause the difference.

**Consequences for the conclusions:**
- "Reminder calls therefore more than halve the DNA rate" (§3) and "Reminder calls have been shown to more than halve DNAs" (§7) are not supported.
- Even if calls had a real effect, the 6.0% applies only to patients who answer and confirm. Calling everyone would not move everyone to 6.0%, so "well within its 8% target" is not a safe projection.

**Suggested fix:** Reword as an association, state the recording limitation explicitly, and recommend a fair test. For example, start recording all call attempts and outcomes, then compare DNA rates by *call attempted* vs *not attempted*. Better still, allocate calls by a rule such as alternate days or sessions for a few months.

### 2. Finding 1 contradicts the memo's own definitions

- §1: late cancellations are "recorded and reported separately."
- §5: the 1,140 late cancellations are "in addition to the DNAs above."
- §6, Finding 1: "The DNA rate of 10.5% (**including late cancellations, which we classify as DNAs**)."

The 10.5% (2,610 / 24,860) **excludes** late cancellations. If they were included, the rate would be (2,610 + 1,140) / 24,860 = **15.1%**. The parenthetical needs to be deleted or corrected. As it stands, it undermines the careful definitional work the memo is otherwise built on.

### 3. "No additional cost" is contradicted by the memo's own figures

- Current volume: 300 calls/week × 4 min = **20 hours/week**.
- Proposed volume: about 960 calls/week × 4 min = **64 hours/week**, an extra **44 hours/week** of reception time. That is more than one full-time post.
- Unanswered calls, which are currently unrecorded, also take time, so the real figure is probably higher.
- Calls are currently made only "where time allows," which suggests reception does not have spare capacity even now.

The claim that this "can be absorbed within existing reception hours at no additional cost" needs evidence or should be removed. A fairer framing would set roughly 44+ reception hours/week against the clinical time potentially recovered. Given issue 1, that recovered time is itself uncertain.

## Moderate issues

- **Cost framing.** £80,900 is the value of clinical time, not cash saved. Clinicians may use DNA slots for notes or admin. Say "the value of clinical time in unused slots" and avoid implying a budget saving.
- **Late cancellations are not costed.** 69% of 1,140 late cancellations were not refilled. That is about 787 slots, roughly 393 hours, or about **£24,400** at the same rate. Including this would strengthen the case for Recommendation 3.
- **Recommendation 3 may need funding.** An automated text system could have licence or integration costs. If the memo, or the covering message, says the recommendations need no new funding, check that this is true here.
- **"Patients" vs "appointments."** Table 2 counts appointments, but the text says "patients who received a reminder call were less than half as likely…". One patient can have many appointments, so use "appointments" throughout.
- **"Within six months" (§7)** has no supporting basis. Either justify it or soften it.

## Minor points

- §4 is sound: 104 of 160 (65%) discharged. Recommendation 2 is sensible and proportionate. It might help to state the target (e.g., 100% reviewed, with documented reasons for non-discharge).
- Note that January–June may not represent the full year (seasonal illness, holidays).
- §1 could state how many staff were interviewed at each site.

## Suggested revised wording

**§3, final paragraph:**
> Appointments where the patient answered a reminder call and confirmed attendance had a DNA rate of 6.0%, compared with 12.5% for all other appointments. Because only answered, confirmed calls are recorded, and calls were made only when staff had time, this comparison is likely to overstate the effect of calls. It does not show how much calls reduce DNAs.

**Recommendation 1:**
> Record all reminder call attempts and outcomes, and test the effect of calls in a structured way (e.g., by session or day) over three months before deciding whether to extend them. Extending calls to all appointments would need around 44 additional reception hours per week, which should be costed.

**§7:**
> Missed appointments cost the service around £80,900 of clinical time every six months, with a further £24,400 from unfilled late cancellations. Reminder calls are associated with lower DNA rates, but the current data cannot show how large their effect is. The discharge-policy and cancellation-list changes can proceed now; the case for extending reminder calls should be tested first.

## Summary

| Issue | Severity | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Reminder-call comparison biased by recording and selection | Major | Reframe as association; break down by appointment type; propose a fair test |
| Finding 1 says late cancellations are included in 10.5% | Major | Delete or correct (it would be 15.1%) |
| "No additional cost" for about 44 extra hrs/week | Major | Cost it or remove the claim |
| Cost of clinical time presented as a saving | Moderate | Clarify wording |
| Late cancellations not costed | Moderate | Add about £24,400 |
| Patients vs appointments wording | Minor | Use "appointments" |

The data collection is strong, and Recommendations 2 and 3 are well-founded. The memo's credibility depends on not overselling the reminder-call result. If Recommendation 1 rests on it and is later shown not to deliver, that will weaken trust in the rest of the audit.
